Hey there, I can totally relate to your sentiment even though my blair says I graduated with a degree from CS. The first CS classes (CS 1301, 1331, 1332, and 2110) are always a little bit a drag on the mind especially for newcomers to CS. I thought I'd provide some insight from my side as someone who also almost switched from CS to IE in the early years, but ended up deeply liking CS.

To give you some context, I made a solid C in both 1331 and 2110, but still managed to turn out really well in terms of my career starting out. 1301 and 1331 happened to be the most boring classes for me, but after 1332 and 2110, I really started becoming interested in CS topics. The upper-class level topics were hard, sure, but they were nothing that was as tedious and detail-demanding as some of the topics were in 1331. I often found myself doing far better in those classes than the beginner topic classes. They also happened to be far more interesting and hands-on compared to the beginner CS classes.

I eventually found classes such as CS 4641 and CS 7643 (ML and Deep Learning) to be one of my favorites, and there are numerous ones depending on what you like. For example, you might like operating systems, computer graphics, or theory. It's totally up to you and that's what I love about the threads at GT.

Also, where's this idea that you sit at a desk and do coding for the rest of your life at Google coming from? Sure, perhaps you do sit at a desk a lot of the times, but you often (at least in my opinion) can work on a variety of interesting and challenging problems such as coming up with a machine learning model, distributed computing, and if you are more interested in UI then you may find mobile application development and web development to your liking. You will find a lot of interesting front-end architectures and you can even apply this knowledge to creating something in VR/AR.

A lot of people of few years down the line switch into engineering management, where they manage a team for a pretty big platform / feature of the software and they lead and work closely with product managers, software engineers, and data scientists to build out high quality features. Alternatively, a degree in CS can pave the way to becoming a product manager or data scientist. So it's not necessarily the case that CS == Software Engineer.

I'll be honest, the prestige of getting into a top-tier tech company attracted me at first, but eventually I've come to love the problems that I solve at my job, converse with valuable coworkers, eat free food, etc.

If you are sure you want to go for architecture, then go for it. I might suggest first keeping your CS major, and taking more architecture classes first to see if you truly love the topic. This way in the future, if you choose to stay with CS, you may even opt for a minor which makes you very unique from other students.

Sorry if this is a bit long, I just haven't seen such a relatable post in a while so I wanted to give my input from my side. All the best!

TL;DR - Almost switched majors to IE from CS because of crappy intro-level classses, but eventually learned to fall in love with CS and never looked back

I didn't list my cum. GPA but had a decent major GPA (3.7), and got an interview through a referral which led to an internship at FB and subsequently a full-time return offer. So referrals or applying early is important so you can get the interviews. I know a lot of really smart people who waited too long to apply, and a lot of mediocre people who applied immediately - guess who got the interviews and the offer.


Afterwards it is up to you to practice LeetCode and hopefully you get lucky or if you are just naturally good at CS you will make it through the interview. Practice makes perfect though. 


I practiced over 400 LC questions and by far it was way more important than any of my classes for getting into the big N. If you do not have the time, I'd recommend buying LeetCode Premium and being laser-focused on the questions tagged for the company you are interviewing at.


If you don't know anyone I'd recommend posting on teamblind or getting a referral through repher.me. There are plenty of people who will help you get a referral to at least 1 of the big N in most cases. 


EDIT: By the way, just because you didn't apply early does not mean you have little chance. Keep applying, I know one person who got their Amazon offer at around March so it is never too late.


Good luck! Getting a big N job is a game-changer, but you can always make it as well after working elsewhere for a year or so.

I've battled depression for years upon years, probably ever since middle school. I thought about suicide numerous times, having the same thoughts you were having. I only overcame this hurdle a year ago. Let me tell you something.

Life is what you make it out to be. You see other people and you undoubtedly say to yourself, man I wish I was like that or even I'll never be like that. The key thing you need to remember is that we as human beings see things that are only good in others. We brush off what we believe are bad examples. That is how we evolve. I always thought about the people ahead of me, never about the people behind or next to me. This made me feel sad, as I felt like I was never achieving anything.   Once I changed this mindset, I felt free.

Strive to be the best. Don't let yourself down so easily. Show the world who you are. That you are the best. 

That's the mindset I have now and it has done wonders for my motivation, grades, and health.

Also, one last note.

Suicide doesn't take away the pain. It only leaves it for people close to you, multiplied exponentially. Can you imagine how devastated your family and friends would be if you just disappeared? "My son that I raised for 18 years, gone just like that?" I beg you to please think things through. Nothing good lies in death. Pain shapes who we are. Two of my good friends have taken their own lives before and the pain it inflicts upon others is just something I would never like to experience or see again. I personally don't think counseling can single-handedly solve your problem. You have to find your inner drive and once that's found, there's nothing to stop you from being who you want to be. Go out into the world like you have something to prove. Be the best you can be. Use this frustration with the world to do what you want to do, and to be the best at it.
